instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: A single memory-stress experiment on cartservice caused near-total failure across all five shopper flows, including checkout. The injected fault was removed after 3.6 seconds, but errors persisted until recovery at about 41 seconds, and cartservice restarted once. The external guard stopped the experiment; the application-level failure was not contained. Evidence is limited to one short run, so other services remain largely untested.

findings.title: Cartservice resource exhaustion causes a broad shopper-flow outage
findings.evidence: With 110 MB memory stress for one worker, overall impact error rate was 95.93%, peak error rate was 100%, peak p95 was 1127.5 ms, and the run was aborted by the error-rate guard. All five flows were affected: error rates were 88.9% on add_to_cart, 94.4% on product, 97.2% on home, and 100% on view_cart and checkout. cartservice restarted once; the fault was active for 3.6 seconds, but recovery took 41 seconds. Its configured memory limit was 128 Mi and peak CPU throttling was 77.3%.
findings.root_cause: The single cartservice replica has little resource headroom under memory pressure. Its restart and unavailability break requests that depend on cart operations; because cartservice is shared by frontend and checkoutservice, failures propagate across every shopper flow. The low p95 values in some individual flows coincide with very high error rates and therefore do not indicate successful fast responses.
findings.fix_rationale: Increasing cartservice's memory limit addresses the demonstrated resource-exhaustion mechanism while retaining the existing CPU limit. This is a targeted mitigation for the memory-stress failure; it does not provide replica redundancy.
findings.expected_improvement: On the same stress experiment, expect no cartservice restart, substantially fewer cart-dependent request failures, and recovery closer to baseline without a prolonged post-fault error period.

Tested cartservice scores retain the supplied anchors. For untested services, null dimension anchors required judgment; scores generally remain near 60, with frontend and checkoutservice reduced for their measured indirect user-flow impact during the cartservice run. Posture is 60 throughout the scored services because each has one replica, readiness and liveness probes, and CPU/memory limits.
output.planner_review: The planner's prediction was confirmed: it predicted all five affected flows, high errors, severe slowdown, and an aborted run, and all were observed. The run also showed a cartservice restart and 41-second recovery, consistent with the predicted resource-exhaustion risk. The guard stopped the injected fault after 3.6 seconds, but the prolonged error period shows that this external safety mechanism did not ensure rapid application recovery.
limitations: Only one experiment was run, targeting cartservice with memory stress; other services and failure classes were not directly tested.
The experiment ran on a single-node Kubernetes setup, so results do not establish multi-node behavior or resilience to node failure.
The probe was small and the fault was short; flow-level request counts were limited.

The run reports a 110 MB stress allocation and one cartservice restart, but its recorded cartservice peak memory was 55.5 MiB against a 128 Mi limit; the exact termination mechanism is not established by the supplied measurements.
